## Abstract

Contexts

The invasion of fast growing Phyllostachys edulis (Moso bamboo) into forest is likely further favored by

climate change, creating more transitional regions within forests. Such forest-bamboo transitional zones

provide windows to look at ecological processes driving bamboo’s interaction with competing species across space.

Objectives

We tested the hypothesis that spatial patterns at scales of ecotone and individual stems can inform

bamboo’s invasive spread and its competitive engulfing strategy, with the allocation of biomass and

resources within a bamboo colony being a key life-history strategy to facilitate its spatial spread.

Methods

We used remote sensing imagery and field survey data to analyze the dynamics of bamboo-tree transitional

boundaries in Tianmu Mountain Nature Reserve (TMNR) of southeastern China. We evaluated bamboo’s

invasive spread and its allocation of resources along the transitional gradient.

Results

Both remote sensing and field data showed bamboo recovery and advancement into tree territories after the

extensive logging of bamboo but with a slower spread compared to historical records. The spatial

distributions of bamboo and tree stems were not random at their transitional interfaces and were affected

by competition. Successful invasion of bamboo required close coordination between stems and rhizomes within a colony, as they served different functions in clonal integration.

Conclusions

Our study initiates a mechanistic, scale-dependent analysis of bamboo invasion strategies, which provides

insights on how to accurately predict future bamboo distributions under climate change accounting for

interspecific competition and bamboo’s clonal integration of resources.

## Introduction

Temporal and spatial shifts in species distribution under global climate change has been an important topic as it connects current ecological patterns to future predictions guiding conservation and policymaking. On

the other hand, while the climate is arguably the most dominant factor controlling species distribution, other

factors such as interspecific competition might limit species distribution to climate-defined potential

habitats. Research on the relative importance of abiotic factors and species interactions on species range

shifts has found that the effect of species interactions varies widely depending on the strength and direction of those interactions (Angert et al. 2013; Louthan et al. 2015). Species with superior growth and

those less adaptive to new abiotic conditions or biotic environments as climate change progresses

(Alexander et al. 2015). Interestingly, these species usually have high invasive potential and are already

abundant and widespread with broad climatic tolerances (Whitney and Gabler 2008; Hellmann et al. 2019).

Clonal plants, such as bamboos, are prevalent in many ecosystems and are well known for their success in

habitats with frequent disturbances and poor resources. Many invasive plant species have clonal growth

forms (Song et al. 2013), expanding their crowns and roots by placing leaves and roots along horizontal stems or rhizomes (Noble et al. 1979). Such growth forms are present in individual plants (i.e., genets) that

produce genetically identical but potentially independent individuals (i.e., ramets) that are physiologically

connected by vegetative growth (Herben and Klimesova 2019). Bamboo is a representative example of

clonal plants that are dominant worldwide with high invasive capacity, especially bamboo species with extensive rhizome networks allowing them to spread quickly by vegetative propagation (Beziquia et al.

2019). Among woody bamboo species capable of reaching forest canopies and forming monospecific

stands, Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) has gained the most attention for its invasion into native

forest communities due to its ecological impacts on forest community structure and carbon dynamics (Li et

al. 1998a; Xu et al. 2017; Chen et al. 2021a). The species is native to China but has been introduced globally (Komatsu et al. 2012; Beziquia et al. 2019), and it has been recorded in successful invasion of secondary

forests, clearings, and edges while replacing native tree species (Kaufman and Kaufman 2013). The 9th

National Forestry Inventory in China (2014–2018) confirmed the expansion of bamboo-dominant areas as

the total bamboo area increased by 113% from 3.00 Mha in 1972 to 6.41 Mha in 2018 (Li and Feng 2019;

Chen et al. 2019). While all bamboo-dominated areas accounted for 2.94% of the total forest area in China, 72.96% of these areas were stands of Moso bamboo (Li and Feng 2019). Although the increase in bamboo-

dominated areas might result from the intensive management of Moso bamboo as a fast-growing grass

with high economic returns (Gu 1992), field studies and remote sensing analyses have detected bamboo

invasion in many nature reserves and protected forest areas (Mertens et al. 2008; Komatsu et al. 2012;

Wang et al. 2016). Moso bamboo invasion was found in coniferous, deciduous, as well as mixed evergreen broadleaf forests (Liu et al. 2011; Shen et al. 2016; Tian et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2021a,b; Chen et al. 2022),

with evergreen broadleaf forests showing the highest vulnerability to bamboo invasion (Ying et al. 2016; Xu

et al. 2019).

Two main factors are central to our study; the first is resource sharing within a bamboo colony. The invasive

spread of Moso bamboo is fueled by its clonal integration (de Kroons and van Groenendael 1997), which is

the resource exchange among bamboo stems (culms) connected via rhizomes that are genetically identical but physiologically distinct. In the period of sprouting, the rapid growth of a new shoot is supported by

water (Fang et al., 2019) as well as carbohydrates from other established stems in the colony rather than from its own photosynthesis (Shi et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2013; Li et al. 1998 a,b). Wang et al. (2016) verified

that culm growth is independent of local light availability, supporting the clonal integration hypothesis in bamboo, as low radiation levels triggered signals to induce resource allocation from the mother plant to the clonal shoots (Reinhart et al., 2006). As old culms age, break or become damaged, new shoots are recruited

to replace them. Rhizomes thus provide nutrients for shoot development during recruitment, while soluble carbohydrates from foliage’s photosynthesis feed into rhizome growth and regeneration. The distribution

Therefore, the rhizome serves a critical role in coordinating bamboo’s growth and expansion above and below ground. However, the complicated nature of rhizome networks and the

challenge of identifying physiologically connected clones within a bamboo stand has created barriers to advance research on translocation dynamics of nutrients, water, and stored nonstructural carbohydrates

(NSC) within a bamboo colony at a fine scale. Unfortunately, few studies have investigated the linkage between biomass and resource allocation within a bamboo colony and bamboo’s invasive spread or evaluated bamboo’s clonal integration of resources as a competitive strategy for invasion.

The second main factor for consideration is competition. So far, a few mechanisms of competition have been proposed from studies on Moso bamboo. Since scientific interest mainly focused on competition for

aboveground light and belowground nutrient and water, the mechanisms of interest were usually examined at the level of physiological individuals with roots, rhizomes, stems, and photosynthetic organs (Chen et al.

2021). However, we still lack a mechanistic understanding of how bamboo as a population of clones can successfully establish and survive in native forests where coinhabiting tree species are usually in control of the canopy. A few studies have attempted to restore the full process of bamboo replacing native tree

species as it invades: Okutomi et al. (1996) proposed that bamboo developed rhizomes at the periphery of native forests and increased culm density at the boundary, waiting to rapidly occupy the open canopy space

created by the death of existing trees. Isagi and Torri (1997) found that Moso bamboo formed a uniform monolayer within competing stands, suppressing seedling recruitment beneath its own canopy, which was consistent with observations from various studies on how bamboo perpetuated its dominance by

eliminating tree recruitment (Taylor and Zisheng 1988; Griscom and Ashton 2003). Zhang and Xue (2018) analyzed competitive relationships between bamboo and native trees using the spatial distribution of stems

as marked point patterns. Their analysis identified spatial interactions between competing bamboo and trees and demonstrated that bamboo clusters around mature trees might contribute to bamboo patch expansion. Their fine-scale analysis of patterns at the transitional interface between bamboo and trees is

informative on underlying ecological processes and mechanisms, but it is still incomplete without analyzing spatial shifts at a larger scale. As a clonal organism functioning at the level of individuals as well as the

level of an integrated population, bamboo requires a cross-scale analysis to connect its spatial distribution of clones to its allocation of growth and resources among them to enable rapid expansion. Therefore, bamboo invasion fronts, which are transitional boundaries between bamboo and native trees provide a

window to investigate ecological processes producing patterns of expansion at broad and fine spatial scales and the role of interspecific competition in bamboo’s range shifts.

Tianmu Mountain Nature Reserve (TMNR) of Zhejiang Province in southeastern China has long been a site of interest for research on bamboo. Multiple remote sensing and census studies have found significant

expansion in the bamboo stand area in the past 30 years. For example, Ding et al. (2006) documented an expansion rate of 4.47 ha per between 1985 and 2003 using remote sensing analysis. Ying et al. (2016) also found bamboo stands in TMNR have expanded at the rate of 7.8 and 26.1 ha per year for the last two

decades, respectively. Therefore, we used bamboo-dominated areas in TMNR as a case study to examine these cross-scale patterns at bamboo’s invasion fronts since multiple studies have documented bamboo

expansion within TMNR throughout the last two decades.

## Methods

## Study area

The study area was in Tianmu Mountain National Nature Reserve (TMNR), Zhejiang Province, southeastern China, established in 1986 as a protected area. Located in mid-latitudes (30°19ʹ N–30°25ʹ N, 119°24ʹ E–

119°29ʹ E), the region is influenced by the southeastern monsoon in the subtropical humid zone of China. The dominant forests are evergreen, deciduous, and mixed broadleaf forests (Ying et al. 2016). Besides, conifer and Moso bamboo stands originally cultivated by monks are important components in the TMNR

forest community. Local climate conditions with mild temperatures (mean annual temperature is 16.8°C in the recent decade; the warmest month and coldest month mean temperatures are 24°C and 3°C,

respectively) and abundant annual precipitation (1390–1870 mm) are considered favorable for bamboo growth (Song et al. 2013).

While human activities within the reserve, i.e., lodging, have been prohibited since 1986, personal communication with local officials informed of occasional thinning activities of bamboo stand invading the

native forests, with the last significant logging effort occurring in 2015. Unfortunately, no official record exists concerning the management of the local bamboo stands to facilitate our study. Despite human intervention in bamboo expansion, thinned bamboo stands appeared to have recovered during data

collection in 2021, which will be assessed and discussed in this research. Remote sensing methods

Our remote sensing workflow closely followed the methods of Ying et al. (2016), which examined the same area for 1984–2015. Three Landsat OLI-8 Level 1 images (on 2014-03-16, 2018-03-11, and 2021-03-26)

Training data points were combined from GPS coordinates of field observations and visually inspected samples from the Google Earth imagery (10-m resolution), with

each sample containing seven band values extracted from the Landsat OLI-8 images at the same time period (see figure S1). Subsequently, for each Landsat image, strata were classified according to five

All statistical analyses were done in R version 4.2.1 (R Core Team 2022). Dynamics at bamboo-tree transitional interface

During the observational period, the transitional boundary between bamboo and trees could be in one of the three scenarios: 1) moving towards trees 2) moving towards bamboo 3) static. These situations signal that

1) bamboo has successfully expanded and invaded into trees 2) bamboo has retreated 3) bamboo has not

invaded into trees. Each potential scenario can be tested on two scales. While the analysis of classified

satellite images summarizes distributional dynamics at the ecotone-level, the age and size distribution of individual bamboo culms and tree stems along the transitional gradient demonstrate the underlying

ecological processes at the stand-level. We expect results at both spatial scales to be consistent regarding

the movement of bamboo’s invasion front. If bamboo has encroached into native forests, younger bamboo age groups are expected to occur more likely at or above the invasion front further into trees, while a mix of

tree sizes would occur at the boundary. If bamboo has retreated or trees have moved into bamboo, we

expect to see trees with smaller sizes and a mix of bamboo age groups at the boundary. If the transitional boundary has been relatively static, a mix of bamboo age groups and tree sizes are expected. Spatial point pattern analysis

The location of all stems along the transects can be analyzed as bi-variate spatial point process with two discrete categories (bamboo and trees). The engulfing strategy of bamboo implies that a higher density of

can secure the open gap rapidly once trees fall. In order to support this hypothesis, we first test if observed spatial point patterns can be distinguished from patterns generated under completely random dispersal

of clones, we expect the spatial point patterns to be significantly different from random patterns.

## Discussion

The natural propagation of bamboos is mainly asexual (Uchimura 1980), and most woody bamboo has

massive flowering and fruiting at intermittent intervals synchronized within a species across large areas (Keeley and Bond 1999). P. edulis has a long flowering interval at around 60 years and is monocarpic, with

all clones in the population dying after flowering and seeding (Janzen 1976). When the canopy became

open during bamboo’s reproduction, tree seedlings and saplings suppressed in the understory of bamboo could successfully re-establish and prevent bamboo seedlings to control the canopy (Griscom and Ashton

2003). Since bamboo has more localized dispersal (Keely and Bond 1999), a greater canopy area before

reproduction will increase the probability of successful regeneration by concentrating more bamboo seeds directly beneath the canopy as bamboo fecundity is usually proportional to its collective crown area

(Norghauer et al. 2011; Qiu et al. 2021). A long waiting time until reproduction thus wins time for P. edulis to

develop extensive rhizomes and increase the total crown area by sprouting new shoots. Unlike many

invasive species relying on aggressive drops of seeds into patches of resident species to establish (Harris et al. 2011; Yang et al. 2015), P. edulis deploys an area-filling strategy for invasion likely due to the lack of

secondary xylem placing itself at a disadvantage in competition with trees at the transitional interface.

Without secondary growth, a bamboo shoot is fixed with its diameter since its germination from the ground and will only exhibit vertical height growth until it reaches maximum height, which is limited both

mechanically and hydraulically (Niklas 2007). A bamboo shoot cannot widen its stem and thus cannot

support extensive branching or broaden its crown (Trujillo and Lopez 2020). Meanwhile, bamboo’s lack of ability to repair xylem or develop new xylem also constrains its maximum height due to hydraulic resistance

(Yang et al. 2021). In comparison, woody species can continue to widen stems and provide structural

support for larger crowns and more photosynthetic organs as they grow (Shinozaki et al. 1964). Therefore,

bamboo can only outcompete trees in the canopy by having a high density of standing stems to add up its collective crown area. When bamboo’s stand density is low, it is likely to be shaded by taller trees with larger

crowns. Even if the bamboo colony can sustainably allocate resources to support that stem in the

understory until a gap finally becomes available from fallen trees, one bamboo stem with limited crown expansion and height will be unlikely to exclude tree growth from the ground and from other existing trees in

the gap. However, if a cluster of bamboo stems can grasp the gap promptly either by lurking in the tree

while the average distance between these bamboo clusters and nearest trees was also shorter than

expected under CSRI. Therefore, once trees at the boundary fall, the surrounding bamboo clusters could fill gaps quickly. In addition, both trees and bamboos were found to be hyperdispersed from the more dominant

type at two ends of the transitional gradient, possibly due to density-regulated mortality effects under

crowding (Harms et al. 2000; Beckman, Neuhauser and Muller-Landau 2012). The competitive dominance of bamboo might have prevented effective tree recruitment within bamboo stands by understory

suppression; likewise, higher density of trees might have thwarted bamboo vegetative spread inside treedominant zones. However, bamboo still had one great advantage over trees to disperse across the boundary

because its clonal integration allows the maintenance of high conspecific density without self-thinning (1996 Makita; Lima et al.2012; Shi et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2015), while trees have demonstrated stronger selfthinning especially when crowded (Westoby 1984; Weller 1989). Clonal integration of resources in bamboo

has facilitated its spatial strategy, which is highly reliant on density. The location of rhizomes is thus crucial to ensure successful gap capturing via bamboo clusters because rhizomes stored with abundant resources need to be in place well before bamboo shoots can emerge from the ground (Yang et al. 2015). Although a

comprehensive distribution of rhizomes was difficult to obtain from sampling, the aggregated patterns of bamboo stems aboveground could offer some clues because feedbacks exist between physiologically

connected rhizomes and stems. Rapid rhizome growth was usually followed by an increase in shoot size (Li et al. 2021), and bamboo culms greater in DBH often had greater productivity and thus contributed to higher return in rhizome growth. The three transition interfaces in our study demonstrated different spatial

distribution of rhizomes: rhizomes appeared to concentrate closer to trees in transect 2 compared to rhizomes in transects 1 and 3. The trend is also consistent with the more visible spatial shift of bamboo-tree boundary in transect 2 as well as the higher relative frequency of youngest bamboo culms within zones of

native trees. The transitional interface acts like a floodgate while bamboo’s invasive potential functions as water potential, and bamboo spread is thus determined by resistance in trees characterized by their density, size, and location as well as the mobility of bamboo realized via strong rhizome dispersal. Our bamboo

distribution in three transects showed that when bamboo transitioned gradually (in transects 1 and 3) and more abruptly (in transect 2), the momentum at bamboo’s invasion fronts might be altered accordingly. A higher density of bamboo at the boundary would be more likely to resist tree dispersal, while accumulating

enough resources in rhizomes to start advancing forward.

Our results did not find any significant effect of spatial location along the transitional gradient on bamboo’s allocation to belowground rhizome biomass as expected. This might be due to constraints in our sampling design: it is possible that 90 meters was too short to detect any difference in bamboo’s investment on

rhizome spatially. In addition, our sample size was relatively small due to the destructive, extensive nature of rhizome sampling. Although we could not infer the entire process of resource translocation within the colony, the correlational relationships between tissue density and carbon, nitrogen, or suggested that stems

and rhizomes serve different functions. Tissue density is the amount of structural biomass invested by unit of volume and has been a key trait indicating plant life history strategies (Westoby 1998; Craine et al. 2003).

The plant economic spectrum demonstrates that faster growth rates and more efficient resource acquisition

are usually associated with lower tissue density in leaf, stems, or roots with trade-offs in shorter life span and lower investment in plant defense against disease and herbivory (Poorter, Lambers and Evans 2014; Ryser et al. 1996; Birouste et al. 2014). Overall, the tissue density of stems is smaller than tissue density

belowground, potentially because bamboo culms need to be more active in expanding and maintaining active photosynthetic area to support the colony’s belowground activities. Bamboo’s culm density has been

shown to increase significantly with age, probably due to the thicker fiber walls and parenchyma cells (Liese 1987; Espiloy 1987; Hisham et al. 2006). Even though no previous work has focused on testing whether aging results in increasing rhizome tissue density, rhizomes have been shown to be anatomically similar to

culms (Ito, Miyafuji and Kasuya 2015). As stem and rhizome tissues became denser, total carbon concentrations went up because carbon is a prerequisite for constructing new biomass (Chiariello, Mooney and Williams 1989). The reverse trend in declining nitrogen might be due to translocation of nitrogen to

other parts of rhizomes, which was previously found in clonal plants (Evans 1988; Eckstein and Karlsson 1999). In addition, clonal integration was found to significantly increase nitrogen availability in the rhizosphere of offspring culms but decrease in mother culms through responses of soil microorganisms (Li

et al. 2018). Nitrogen is crucial to increase plants’ photosynthetic performance under low light conditions (Luo et al. 2022), and thus translocation of nitrogen is necessary to balance carbon budget among culms within the colony, especially for young culms waiting in the understory under stronger interspecific

competition. Besides structural carbon, non-structural carbon in the form of starch and soluble sugar are also stored in bamboo stem and rhizomes (Li et al. 2021). As rhizomes become denser, the storage of NSC increases accordingly. The starch concentration is almost 30 times higher than the concentration of soluble

sugar, because free sugar is easier to mobilize than long-term starch storage and thus has a lower content (Wang et al. 2016). Even though stems can serve as short-term storage for NSC when carbon gain exceeds demand, their relationships between tissue density and storage were not as strong as relationships shown

in rhizomes. The allocation patterns in roots appeared to be different from patterns in stems and rhizomes, possibly resulting from their disparate metabolic and physiological functions.

We could examine bamboo’s invasive potential and spreading trends from remote sensing imagery, finescale plant census, and samples on plant nutrients and traits, but we need to be more cautious of human’s

role in the ecology of bamboo. Apart from climatic control, competition with trees assessed and discussed in our study is crucial to bamboo expansion. In addition, human has facilitated bamboo’s colonization of

large areas by introducing bamboo to forests and cultivating extensive stands under intensive management (Fu and Banik 1995), while also contained its spread by massive logging as seen in our study. Current research mainly focuses on how different stand management strategies such as shoot harvesting and

fertilization on bamboo’s productivity or carbon sequestration (Wu et al. 2015; Nath, Lal and Das 2015; Song et al. 2011), but we need long-term monitoring of bamboo invasion fronts as well as better knowledge on land use history to separate human’s effect on bamboo distribution across spatial-temporal scales. Another

challenge in our study was the difficulty to locate transitional boundaries between bamboo and trees, and our transects were established only based on observations made on the ground. Such protocol limited our ability to find more suitable sites and generated bias on bamboo’s directionality of spread as bamboo area

outside each transect could contribute to new growth within each transect. Future research can utilize

## Conclusion

We found that Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) has recovered and expanded after extensive logging in

2015 within Tianmu Mountain National Reserve. The shifting of bamboo invasion fronts was consistent between classified results from remote sensing imagery as well as finer analysis of size and age distributions of stems along the transitional gradients. Even though three transects showed different

extents of bamboo advancement, spatial point pattern analysis confirmed that bamboo’s culm dispersal followed a non-random spatial process influenced by the location of trees. Interactions between bamboo and trees created resistance to dispersal from competing species at the transitional interface. However,

bamboo formed clusters of shoots at the boundary, which might help secure their control of canopy as trees become rare within bamboo-dominant regions and die due to aging or competition. Bamboo stems and rhizomes demonstrated significant correlations between tissue density and resources crucial to growth and

survival. While carbon and nitrogen showed closer associations with growth in culms aboveground, the storage of free sugars and starch was more correlated to rhizome tissue density. Our study was a first step

to connect factors driving bamboo’s invasive potential at different spatial scales together and emphasized the necessity of cross-scale analysis on a typical clonal species ecologically important to forest community structure and functioning.

# RESEARCH

Comparing community birdwatching and professional bird monitoring with implications for avian diversity research: a case study of Suzhou, China

Yan Zhou1,2*  , Anping Chen3*, Jenny Q. Ouyang4, Yanlin Liu5, Aiyu Zheng6, Zaixi Yang1, Yong Zhang1, Bin Wang7, Yifei Jia2, Shengwu Jiao2,8, Qing Zeng2 and Changhu Lu1

Abstract Background:  In the past decades, birdwatching as a hobby developed rapidly and produced ample scientific records that have aided conservation efforts. Therefore, it is increasingly attractive to promote avian research by providing data from birdwatching. Methods:  We compared records from 16 years of community birdwatching and a 1-year formalized bird monitoring in Suzhou, China to study the similarities and differences between the two monitoring methods. Results:  We showed that within the 325 bird species recorded by the two methods, an annual average of 108 species were documented by community science and 223 bird species were recorded by 1-year formalized monitoring. Measured by the number of bird species recorded per survey trip, the bird monitoring activity of community birdwatchers was significantly lower. Furthermore, the monitoring intensity of community birdwatching measured as the average survey trips per site each survey year was also lower than that of formalized bird monitoring. In addition, community birdwatchers preferred urban landscapes to rural areas. Conclusions:  Community birdwatching could record the majority of local birds and complements the professional surveys in avian research. Well designed and coordinated community science can be used to expand the knowledge about avian distribution and population dynamics. These findings are critical for the development of conservation science with regard to community involvement. Keywords:  Avian diversity, Birdwatching, Community science, Conservation, Formalized bird monitoring

Background The term of citizen science refers to scientific investigations and research activities involving non-professionals (Bonney et al. 2014; Kullenberg and Kasperowski 2016),

which was gradually instead of the term of community science for the exclusive connotations surrounding the word citizen (Audubon website 2018). In the past few decades, community science has grown rapidly in ecology and conservation (McKinley et al. 2017). Community science, especially the development in species monitoring, has accumulated a large number of observation records, providing first-hand data for scientific research (Gardiner et al. 2012; Kosmala et al. 2016). Compared to traditional research run by professional researchers, an apparent advantage of community science is its potential

to engage many more participants for long-term research on a wider spatial scale, e.g., in conservation biology and agricultural science research (McKinley et al. 2017; Abbott et al. 2018). Coupled with the rapid development of information technology, such as social networking and messaging platforms, volunteers from different countries and different fields can effectively carry out simultaneous scientific research and monitoring, further highlighting the value of community science (McKinley et al. 2017). However, data quality and distribution from community science can vary due to differing skill levels and frequency of participation so researchers should exercise caution when employing these datasets (Theobald et al. 2015). To use data generated by community science, it is essential to first assess its data quality and usefulness, ideally with the data obtained by professional researchers (Gilfedder et al. 2019). Birds are among the most effective indicator organisms of environmental change because of their rapid response to habitat change (Stephens et al. 2016). Many birds are brightly colored, vocally pleasant, and highly distinguishable between species, making them the most commonly used target organisms for community science activities (Dickinson et al. 2010; Tulloch et al. 2013). As early as the 19th century, the National Audubon Association of the United States carried out systematic birdwatching activities and published a large number of research results based on community birdwatching data. The establishment of the eBird database further enables avian scholars to access and analyze publically available community birdwatching data (Wood et al. 2011; Sullivan et al. 2014). Data from community science can be used to generate long-term trends that could complement data from traditional surveys, and the research on avian species distribution, population dynamics, response to climate change, and the conservation of avian distribution hotspots could also be strengthened using community data (Crick 2010; Hochachka et  al. 2012; Walker and Taylor 2017; Hong et al. 2018; Horns et al. 2018). China is one of the richest countries in avian species diversity (Zheng 2017). However, community bird watchers did not emerge in Chinese mainland until the 1980s (Ma et al. 2013; Walther and White 2018). Since then, a large number of birdwatching enthusiasts have appeared, whose footprints have largely covered all of China (Ma et al. 2013; Walther and White 2018). Enthusiastic community bird watchers often self-upload birdwatching records to the China Bird Recording Center (http:// www.szbir​d.org.cn/birdt​alker​.net/index​.asp) and the China Bird Watching Center (http://www.birdr​eport​.cn/) (Walther and White 2018). These data have already been used for the study of the distribution and population dynamics of birds (Li et  al. 2012; Hu et  al. 2017; Zhou

et al. 2019a, b). However, due to inherent shortcomings of non-professional birdwatching, such as less-skilled birdwatchers, etc. (Bart 2005), the use of community birdwatching data for addressing important scientific questions, such as avian species distribution and diversity, needs careful attention. Currently, comparative studies to assess the quality and scope of the rapidly growing community birdwatching data in China are still lacking, which prevents researchers from appropriately using these data to investigate avian biogeography, population dynamics, and conservation. At present, birdwatching is still a “middle-class activity” in China, which is more often conducted in more prosperous regions (Ma et al. 2013; Wang 2015; Walther and White 2018). Hence, we selected Suzhou, one of the most developed prefecture-level cities in China, as the research area. Suzhou is a developed city in China, located close to the hotspot of migratory birds. Many Suzhou volunteers are enthusiastic birdwatchers with somewhat varied birdwatching willing or skill level, better reflecting Chinese community birdwatching. We conducted a year of formalized bird monitoring in Suzhou. We then compared our formalized data with data obtained from community birdwatching. Our goal was to study the similarities and differences between the two bird monitoring methods, such as checklist and monitoring intensity, and to explore the potential use of community birdwatching data for avian diversity research and conservation.

Methods Survey area Suzhou City (30° 47′‒32° 02′ N, 119° 55′‒121° 20′, Fig. 1) is located in the southeastern part of Jiangsu Province, east of the Taihu Plain in the Yangtze River Delta, with a total area of 8848 km2. Low-elevation (2‒4 m above the sea level) plains account for 54.9% of the city’s total area, followed by water body (42.5% of the total area). The low hills with an altitude of 100‒350 m scatter the west of the city and on the Taihu Island. The Yangtze River and the Beijing-Hangzhou Canal run through the northern part of the city, and the number of rivers and streams reaches more than 20,000. Located in the middle of the migratory route for East Asian-Australasian migratory birds, Suzhou’s abundant wetlands make the area an important wintering ground and stopover for migratory birds (Qi 2008). Suzhou has a subtropical monsoon maritime climate with four distinct seasons. The annual average temperature is 15.7 °C (range: 3.1 °C in January and 28 °C in July). The average annual precipitation is about 1100 mm, concentrated in April to September, with the highest rainfall

Search and collation of community birdwatching records The China Bird Recording Center was launched in 2002 and houses birdwatching records as early as January 1997. The China Bird Watching Center launched in 2014 contains birdwatching records from January 2001 onwards. Both data centers require bird species, number of individuals, location, date, and habitat description for records. We downloaded all bird-watching data records from Suzhou from the two data centers. Some birdwatchers upload the same birdwatching record on both websites, in which case we used one copy from the China Bird Watching Center. We found 471 community birdwatching events which had occurred at 66 sites (Fig. 1) from July 2003 to June 2018. Bird species nomenclature in this study follows Zheng (2017).

Formalized bird survey From July 2017 to June 2018, we conducted the first comprehensive expert survey of bird species and distribution in Suzhou. In doing so, we divided the Suzhou area into 350 5 km × 5 km grids. We chose 38 grids out of the total of 350 grids for the survey, i.e., a sampling intensity of more than 10%. The grid selection was based on pre-survey field scout and local knowledge provided by the local forestry administration to ensure most bird hotspots were covered. The survey covers all bird habitat types in Suzhou, including river wetlands, lake wetlands, hilly woodlands, farmland and urban landscapes (Fig. 1). The 1-year survey also considered the seasonal differences in the avian community in Suzhou and included one full bird migration season. For each surveyed grid, a 2 km-long route was set and the frequency of field investigations was once a month, accumulating to 456 surveys in total. For each field investigation, the team consisted of 2‒3 experienced investigators (at least 5 years of experience). The team was equipped with one single-lens

Data analysis All statistical analyses were conducted with the SPSS program version 18.0. We used non-parametric tests as the distributions of observed species number for community birdwatching failed to pass the normal distribution test. The list length is how many species were recorded in a single trip, which is important information for qualifying the absence of a particular species from a list, reflecting the bird species monitoring effort when all bird checklist are collected from a certain region (Szabo et al. 2010). Consequently, we used the list length as an indicator of the professionalism of community investigators. We used the Mann–Whitney test to assess the difference in the number of bird species per survey trip

between professional bird survey and community birdwatching. In order to better compare the list length from two methods of bird monitoring, we randomly sampled from the professional survey data collected intensively within 1 year (original sample size = 456) to simulate data collected from monthly professional monitoring within 1 year, 5 years, 10 years and 15 years. New sample size was thus 12, 60, 120, 180, respectively. We performed 1000 replicates for all the 4 scenarios to show the percentage of 1000 p values that are significant (p < 0.05) between professional bird survey and community birdwatching. Based on the ratio of the number of surveys to the number of areas surveyed each year, we measured the intensity of annual birdwatching and formalized bird monitoring.

Results During 2002‒2018, the retrieved community birdwatching events documented a total of 305 species in Suzhou. On an average year from July to June, there were about 108.1 (range: 26‒242) species documented by community birdwatching. Compared to the 161 species recorded in 2017‒2018 by community birdwatching, the 1-year professional survey recorded 223 bird species (Fig. 2). Overall, by combining professional survey and community birdwatching records, 325 bird species were recorded in Suzhou. Some 203 bird species were recorded by both professional survey and community birdwatching. For the 102 species of birds recorded by community birdwatchers

On the other hand, among 20 species that were observed in the professional survey but not by community birdwatchers, 11 species were resident birds and 7 species were migrants (Fig. 3). The average number of bird species surveyed per single trip was smaller for community birdwatching than formal bird monitoring (20.24 ± 14.14 species by community birdwatchers, 21.30 ± 7.76 by professionals, p < 0.01; Mann–Whitney test). The random sampling also shows that formal bird monitoring has a longer list length than community birdwatching (Fig. 4). The distribution of list length for a single survey showed a normal distribution pattern for formalized bird monitoring, while the list length of a single trip by community birdwatchers enormously varies and shows a “tailed distribution” (Fig. 5). The annual average list length of community birdwatching varies in different monitoring years, ranging between 6.55 (2008‒2009) and 28.91 (2015‒2016) (Fig.  6). For years with community birdwatching survey numbers greater than 50 (2007‒2008, 2013‒2014, 2014‒2015, and 2015‒2016), a Mann–Whitney test shows that only 2015‒2016 had a significant difference in average list length between birdwatching and monitoring (p < 0.01). Both formalized bird monitoring and community birdwatching focused more on lake habitats (Table  1), and both methods differed little in monitoring intensities for river and woodland landscape. Compared with formalized bird monitoring, community birdwatching was more likely to be carried out in urban landscapes and not conducted in the farmland area (Table 1). Over the 1-year formalized bird monitoring period, there were 456 survey trips for the professionally

investigated 38 survey sites, indicating once a month per site (Fig. 7). In comparison, there were a total of 471 survey trips for all community birdwatching trips combined over a span of 16 years at 66 survey sites (Fig. 7). Furthermore, the monitoring intensity ranged between 1 and 3.3 by community birdwatching from 2002‒2003 to 2017‒2018, in comparison to 12 by the professional survey. Compared with the consistent monitoring intensity of the professional survey, the monitoring intensity of community birdwatching fluctuates monthly (Fig. 8).

Discussion Community science in bird surveys, such as the eBird database for the United States, has allowed scientists to answer questions in avian population ecology and conservation biology, but birdwatching has only been active for the past two decades in China. As a result, the databases for bird counts have not been checked and validated with scientific monitoring. We attempted to address this lack by comparing data from community science birdwatching and professional monitoring. We found that although the number of bird species recorded by birdwatching per year increased over the past two decades, community bird monitoring is influenced by personal activity of birdwatching, monitoring site selection, and lack of consistence, which may result in biased results for formal inquiries. Over the past 16 years, community birdwatchers have recorded a total of 305 species of birds, including several rare species that are occasionally seen in Suzhou, such as the Scaly-sided Merganser (Mergus squamatus) and the Black-faced Spoonbill (Platalea minor). Moreover, many years of continuous community engagement in birdwatching can cover a broader area than professional surveys that are often limited by people and funding. The intensity of professional surveys sometimes is lower than that of community birdwatching at some hotspots of birdwatching. This broad spatial and temporal coverage allows community birdwatchers to record occasionally migratory bird species that are less likely to be encountered by formalized bird monitoring in a short period. Records of community birdwatching also revealed at least four species of birds that have never been recorded in the Jiangsu Province before, including Rufous-faced Warbler (Abroscopus albogularis), Common Ringed Plover (Charadrius hiaticula), and Verditer Flycatcher (Eumyias thalassinus) (Yang et al. 2018; Huang et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2019a, b). Overall, our results suggest that community birdwatching well complements the expensive professional surveys in investigating and monitoring bird resources and their spatio-temporal dynamics especially

The remaining 9 resident birds not recorded by community birdwatching are Collared Crow (Corvus torquatus), Barred Owlet (Glaucidium cuculoides), Greater Barbet (Megalaima virens), Oriental Scops Owl (Otus sunia), Plumbeous Water-redstart (Rhyacornis fuliginosus), Striated Prinia (Prinia criniger), Lesser Necklaced Laughingthrus (Garrulax monileger), Blue Whistling-thrush (Myophonus caeruleus) and Grey-headed Woodpecker (Picus canus). Therefore, the current intensity and seasonal coverage of community birdwatching in Suzhou is not sufficient to reflect the seasonal dynamics of bird species in different types of landscapes. In addition, the activity of community birdwatchers is highly uneven, reflected in the fact that the species list length of singletrip records varies greatly (SD = 14.14, Fig. 6) and most of the list length of community birdwatching are less than that of formalized bird survey (Figs.  4 and 5), indicating that the birdwatching activities of many community scientists need to be strengthened or well-designed and birdwatching plan should be employed when watching birds. Besides personal activity of birdwatching, the difference between males and females, adults and juveniles, and the difference of birdwatching distance could impact the checklist of both community birdwatching and formalized bird survey, which was not taken into account in this study. Control experiments need to be run in future studies to clearly demonstrate the accurate differences between the two methods. The extensive engagement of community birdwatching has become a highly useful tool in supplement to formalized bird monitoring, although the results of this study indicate that there are still various deficiencies in the current community birdwatching. Moreover, with careful planning and training, community birdwatchers can be organized to work along with professional ornithological researchers and become a part of formalized bird monitoring (Bai et al. 2015; Zeng et al. 2018). For example, well-designed community birdwatching plans such as the Christmas Bird Count (CBC) by eBird and the North American Breeding Bird Survey (NA-BBS) led by the USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center and many other organizations have provided researchers with a large amount of reliable monitoring data (Sauer and Link 2011; Amano et al. 2018). In China, universities, research institutions, and professional organizations have also started to provide ornithological training courses and organize students and amateurs to carry out bird monitoring (Ma et al. 2013). Examples include the Survey of the Yellow Sea Waterbirds by the Wetland International China Office in collaboration with multiple universities (Chen et al. 2019) and the China Coastal Waterbirds Synchronization Survey organized by China Coastal Waterbird Census Group (Bai et al. 2015). The integration of

community birdwatching with professional efforts has greatly expanded the monitoring network for China’s bird species, and found dozens of bird species that have never been recorded in China (Liu et al. 2013). Nevertheless, there is still a long way to go before largescale applications of community birdwatching records (Ma et al. 2013). At present, the main problems faced by Chinese bird watchers include the lack of bird watching organizations, the shortage of funds, and the lack of communication between birdwatchers. In order to cope with these problems, some environmental protection foundations in China, such as the SEE Foundation, have begun to systematically cultivate birdwatching organizations through financial and intellectual support. Some environmental agencies such as the Shan Shui Conservation Center and the China Birdwatching Association have launched national-scale species monitoring programs such as China Nature Watch, National Wintering Survey of Scaly-sided Merganser, which organizes birdwatchers for endangered birds monitoring (Zeng et al. 2018). The development of birdwatching in China is also in sync with the rapid development of network technology. China’s earliest birdwatching website and eBird were launched in 2002, and many birdwatchers learned to publicly share their data. However, not all birdwatchers observe and record important population and habitat information, such as the number of individual species, behavioral and habitat data, other than just recording the species name. This lack of inconsistence of important information could prevent researchers from conducting in-depth analyses of community birdwatching data. In the future, with the development of China’s economy, we can expect to see more and more birdwatchers (Sekercioglu 2002). More resources need to be invested to maximize the scientific literacy of the birdwatchers, and to satisfy their curiosity about nature and bird species. We also need to enable close communications between birdwatchers and professional researchers, so that more bird research can benefit from the development of birdwatching with the help of big data technology.

Conclusions Our study suggests that the current intensity of community birdwatching could record the majority of local birds and complements the expensive professional surveys in investigating and monitoring avian resources and species spatio-temporal dynamics. Meanwhile, the imbalance of personal activity of birdwatching and spatio-temporal distribution of community birdwatching limits the extensive utilization of community birdwatching in avian research.
